content: 1. Members of an LGBT community organization in Los Angeles, particularly men who have sex with men (MSM), were studied to understand their engagement with HIV-related care. This research was published in the Journal of the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care in 2017, highlighting the importance of community-based approaches to HIV prevention and care. 2. Meyerson et al. (2013) explored the perspectives of pharmacists regarding over-the-counter rapid HIV tests. Their findings, published in AIDS and Behavior, emphasized the potential for pharmacists to play a more active role beyond simply selling the tests, including providing education and support for self-testing. 3. Mugo et al. (2017) conducted a feasibility study in Kenya to assess the uptake and acceptability of oral HIV self-testing among clients of community pharmacies. The study, published in PLOS ONE, demonstrated that self-testing could be a viable option for expanding HIV testing services in resource-limited settings. 4. Myers et al. (2017) investigated the availability, accessibility, and pricing of rapid HIV self-tests in New York City pharmacies during the summer of 2013. Their research, published in AIDS and Behavior, provided insights into the barriers and facilitators of self-testing in urban settings. 5. Ng et al. (2012) evaluated the accuracy and user acceptability of oral fluid-based HIV rapid self-tests. Published in PLOS ONE, the study highlighted the reliability of these tests and their potential to increase testing rates among populations at risk. 6. Ngure et al. (2017) examined the feasibility and acceptability of HIV self-testing among pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) users in Kenya. Their findings, published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, underscored the role of self-testing in supporting PrEP adherence and monitoring. 7. Nour et al. (2012) demonstrated that patients in emergency department settings could accurately perform their own rapid HIV point-of-care tests. This study, published in Point of Care: The Journal of Near-Patient Testing & Technology, highlighted the potential for self-testing in high-stress environments. 8. Offorjebe et al. (under review) analyzed the acceptability of HIV self-testing for index partner testing among HIV-positive clients in Malawi. Their mixed-methods study provided valuable insights into the role of self-testing in partner notification and linkage to care. 9. Okoboi et al. (2019) conducted a qualitative study in Uganda to assess the acceptability, perceived reliability, and challenges associated with distributing HIV self-test kits to young MSM. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study emphasized the importance of tailored approaches for this population. 10. Pant Pai et al. (2013) explored the feasibility of unsupervised HIV self-testing among healthcare workers in South Africa. Their cross-sectional pilot study, published in PLOS ONE, demonstrated the potential for self-testing to address barriers to testing in healthcare settings. 11. Pant Pai et al. (2017) conducted a cross-sectional survey in Canada to understand key stakeholders' perspectives on HIV self-testing. Published in AIDS and Behavior, the study highlighted the need for stakeholder engagement in the implementation of self-testing programs. 12. Pilarski et al. (2017) reported on the involvement of users in the co-design of HIV self-testing services. Their findings, presented at a workshop and published in Sexually Transmitted Infections, emphasized the importance of user-centered design in developing effective self-testing interventions. 13. Prazuck et al. (2016) evaluated the use of a finger-stick whole-blood HIV self-test as a screening tool for the general public. Published in PLOS ONE, the study demonstrated the test's adaptability and potential for widespread use. 14. Qin et al. (2017) examined the benefits and potential harms of HIV self-testing among MSM in China. Their implementation-focused study, published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases, provided a nuanced understanding of self-testing's impact on this population. 15. Rosengren et al. (2016) assessed the feasibility of using the Grindr app to distribute HIV self-test kits to MSM in Los Angeles. Published in Sexual Health, the study highlighted the potential of leveraging social networking apps for public health interventions. 16. Sarkar et al. (2016) conducted a mixed-methods study in rural India to evaluate the feasibility of supervised self-testing using oral fluid-based HIV rapid tests among pregnant women. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study emphasized the importance of supervision in ensuring accurate results. 17. Schnall et al. (2016) investigated whether high-risk young adults use HIV self-tests appropriately. Their think-aloud study, published in AIDS and Behavior, provided insights into the usability and acceptability of self-testing among this demographic. 18. Sharma et al. (2017) explored the willingness of MSM in the United States to distribute free rapid home HIV test kits and test with their social or sexual network associates. Published in AIDS Care, the study highlighted the potential for peer-driven testing strategies. 19. Sibanda et al. (2017) conducted a qualitative study and choice experiment in rural Zimbabwe to understand preferences for HIV self-test kit distribution models. Presented at the 9th IAS Conference on HIV Science, the study emphasized the importance of community preferences in designing distribution strategies. 20. Smith et al. (2017) investigated the acceptability of a web-based HIV self-testing service in South Africa. Presented at the IAS Conference on HIV Science, the study highlighted the potential for digital platforms to expand access to self-testing. 21. Stephenson et al. (2018) piloted a video counseling and home-based HIV testing intervention for transgender youth. Presented at the HIV Research for Prevention conference, the study emphasized the importance of tailored interventions for this population. 22. Strauss et al. (2018) examined the preferences of truck drivers in Kenya for oral self-testing as a means to increase HIV testing uptake. Published in BMC Public Health, the study highlighted the potential of self-testing to reach underserved populations. 23. Thirumurthy et al. (2018) assessed the willingness of women in Kenya to pay for HIV self-tests, with implications for subsidy and pricing policies. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study provided insights into the economic aspects of self-testing. 24. Tobin et al. (2018) evaluated the acceptability and feasibility of a peer mentor program to train young Black MSM to promote HIV and STI home-testing within their social networks. Published in AIDS Care, the study highlighted the role of peer-driven approaches in increasing testing rates. 25. Tun et al. (2018) reported on a pilot program in Nigeria that used key opinion leaders to promote HIV self-testing and linkage to treatment among MSM. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study demonstrated the effectiveness of community-based strategies. 26. van Rooyen et al. (2015) examined the constraints and opportunities for scaling up HIV self-testing in Africa, with evidence from Kenya, Malawi, and South Africa. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study provided a comprehensive analysis of implementation challenges. 27. Volk et al. (2016) assessed the acceptability and feasibility of HIV self-testing among MSM in Peru and Brazil. Published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS, the study highlighted the potential for self-testing to reach high-risk populations in Latin America. 28. Witzel et al. (2017) conducted a qualitative study in England to explore the perspectives of key informants on the implementation of HIV self-testing. Published in Sexually Transmitted Infections, the study identified barriers, facilitators, and anticipated impacts of self-testing. 29. Witzel et al. (2019) piloted an internet-based randomized controlled trial targeting MSM and transgender individuals in England and Wales. Published in BMC Infectious Diseases, the study evaluated advertising strategies and the acceptability of the intervention. 30. Wong et al. (2015) investigated the usage and acceptability of HIV self-testing among MSM in Hong Kong. Published in AIDS and Behavior, the study provided insights into the cultural and contextual factors influencing self-testing. 31. Wray et al. (2017) developed a smart home HIV testing kit, eTEST, which enables active, real-time follow-up and referral after testing. Published in JMIR mHealth and uHealth, the study highlighted the potential of technology to enhance self-testing. 32. Yan et al. (2015) explored the experiences and correlates of HIV self-testing among MSM in Jiangsu Province, China. Published in AIDS and Behavior, the study provided valuable insights into the factors influencing self-testing uptake. 33. Zanolini et al. (2018) assessed the acceptability, comprehension of instructions, and preferences for self-test kit distribution among adolescents and adults in Zambia. Published in AIDS Research & Human Retroviruses, the study emphasized the importance of user-friendly designs. 34. Zerbe et al. (2015) evaluated the acceptability and uptake of home-based HIV self-testing in Lesotho. Presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, the study highlighted the potential for self-testing to increase testing rates in rural settings. 35. Zhong et al. (2017) examined the acceptability and feasibility of a social entrepreneurship model to promote HIV self-testing among MSM. Published in HIV Medicine, the study emphasized the role of innovative approaches in expanding access to testing. 36. Nguyen et al. (2019) reported on community-led HIV self-testing in Vietnam, demonstrating its success in reaching key populations and their partners. Presented at the 10th IAS Conference on HIV Science, the study highlighted the importance of community involvement. 37. Matovu et al. (2017) conducted a qualitative study in Uganda to explore perceptions of female partner-delivered HIV self-testing among pregnant women and their male partners. Published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS, the study emphasized the role of partner involvement in testing. 38. Figueroa et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the reliability of HIV rapid diagnostic tests for self-testing versus testing by healthcare workers. Published in The Lancet HIV, the study provided evidence for the accuracy of self-testing. 39. Mangenah et al. (2019) performed an economic cost analysis of door-to-door community-based distribution of HIV self-test kits in Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study highlighted the cost-effectiveness of this approach. 40. Ahmed et al. (2018) analyzed the costs of differentiated HIV self-testing kit distribution in Zambia. Presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, the study provided insights into the financial implications of scaling up self-testing. 41. Medley et al. (2019) compared the outcomes and costs of three methods for increasing male partner testing in South Africa. Presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, the study emphasized the importance of cost-effective strategies. 42. Huang et al. (2015) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of promoting HIV self-testing through Grindr™, a smartphone social networking app. Published in Sexually Transmitted Infections, the study demonstrated the potential of digital platforms for public health interventions. 43. Cambiano et al. (2015) assessed the potential impact and cost-effectiveness of self-testing for HIV in low-income countries. Published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, the study provided a comprehensive analysis of the economic benefits of self-testing. 44. Cambiano et al. (2017) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of different delivery approaches for HIV self-testing. Presented at the 24th Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, the study highlighted the importance of tailored strategies. 45. Cambiano et al. (2019) conducted a health economic and modeling analysis to assess the impact and cost-effectiveness of community-based HIV self-testing in sub-Saharan Africa. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study emphasized the potential for self-testing to improve health outcomes. 46. Indravudh et al. (2019) developed a study protocol for a cluster-randomized trial to evaluate community-led delivery of HIV self-testing in rural Malawi. Published in BMC Infectious Diseases, the study aimed to improve HIV testing and broader social outcomes. 47. Yang et al. (in press) discussed the role of people-centered social innovation in Asian HIV services, focusing on key populations and their empowerment. The study emphasized the importance of community-driven approaches. 48. The WHO consolidated guidelines on self-care interventions for health, including sexual and reproductive health and rights, provide comprehensive recommendations for implementing self-testing. These guidelines were accessed in September 2019. 49. The WHO guidance on couples HIV testing and counseling, including antiretroviral therapy for serodiscordant couples, offers a public health approach to improving testing and treatment. Published in 2012, the guidelines remain a critical resource. 50. Semple et al. (2018) evaluated the uptake of a partner notification model for HIV among MSM and transgender women in Tijuana, Mexico. Published in AIDS and Behavior, the study highlighted the importance of partner notification in increasing testing rates. 51. Little et al. (2019) shared insights from the scale-up of an HIV-assisted partner notification intervention in Central Asia. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study emphasized the challenges and successes of implementation. 52. Carballo-Diéguez et al. (2002) investigated the intention to notify sexual partners about potential HIV exposure among clients of New York City STD clinics. Published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases, the study provided insights into partner notification behaviors. 53. Baytop et al. (2014) compared strategies to increase HIV testing among African-American gay, bisexual, and other MSM in Washington, DC. Published in AIDS Care, the study highlighted the effectiveness of targeted interventions. 54. Cabrera Oliva et al. (2018) examined whether online interventions could enhance HIV case finding and linkage to care. Presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference, the study compared online and offline monitoring data. 55. Clark et al. (2014) compared sampling methodologies for epidemiologic surveillance of MSM and transgender women in Latin America. Published in AIDS and Behavior, the study provided empirical evidence for the effectiveness of different approaches. 56. Ellen et al. (2014) evaluated recruitment approaches for identifying newly diagnosed HIV infections among African Americans. The study emphasized the importance of targeted recruitment strategies.
